[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on this. Maya will drive the technical bits.
[00:12] Maya Patel: Hi team, hey Alex, Priya, Tom. We'll start with a quick recap of what you sent—your baseline model is the 13B transformer running on a dual-GPU edge box, right?
[00:22] Alex Chen: Yep, that's right, it's a trimmed variant we use on the robot fleet. It's currently FP16 in production, and we're looking to do INT8 or even FP8 to save cycles.
[00:34] Maya Patel: Cool. So agenda: INT8/FP8 accuracy, then GPTQ vs AWQ conversion tradeoffs, runtime implications for KV cache and batching, and lastly deployment constraints for VPC/on-prem.
[00:45] Tom Ruiz: Sounds good. We primarily care about endpoint latency under 60ms p95 and minimal regressions on our control/command classification tasks.
[00:56] Maya Patel: Understood. Quick note: when we talk about "regression" here we'll use both intrinsic metrics like perplexity and task-level accuracy on your 100 prompt set. Sometimes lower perplexity doesn't map 1:1 to task accuracy, so we always recommend task evals.
[01:10] Priya Nair: Also, network-wise for on-prem, we can't allow outbound model artifacts; so any benchmarking needs to happen inside our VPC or via a secure data lane.
[01:20] Jordan Lee: Right, we documented that in the security pack, and we can run the bench in your VPC via the Private deployment. We'll note that as a constraint.
[01:30] Maya Patel: Ok jumping into INT8 vs FP8 — INT8 gives great memory and throughput improvements on Ampere/A100 style GPUs if kernels are optimized, but it's more likely to induce accuracy delta unless you use GPTQ-style per-channel quant. AWQ (the new adaptive-weight quant) often gives better accuracy for certain layers but can be slower to convert and tooling is still maturing.
[01:52] Alex Chen: Can you remind me — GPTQ is the chunked quantization that does per-channel scale, right? I remember reading about it but haven't run it on our model.
[02:02] Maya Patel: Yes, GPTQ does per-channel and is often done with a small calibration dataset to minimize LLM regressions. AWQ is a newer technique that sometimes mixes 4-bit-like packing with special handling for outlier weights; on some models AWQ can beat GPTQ in task accuracy, but conversion tooling differs.
[02:22] Tom Ruiz: Practical question — what's the expected latency delta when moving from FP16 to INT8 or FP8 assuming same runtime?
[02:29] Maya Patel: It depends. INT8 can improve throughput and reduce memory bandwidth so headroom for batching increases — so you might see 20-40% lower per-token cost and latency improvements in high concurrency. But for single-stream p95 latency it's mixed; if kernels aren't optimized you can even see small regressions due to dequant/depack overhead. FP8 on supported runtimes with fused kernels (fp8 compute path) can be ~10-25% faster than FP16 with better memory savings, but hardware support (and our runtime kernel set) matters.
[02:56] Alex Chen: Our biggest concern is not throughput per se, it's jitter on p95 that makes control commands flaky.
[03:03] Maya Patel: Then we'd prioritize low-burst-latency modes: smaller batch sizes, enabling KV cache warmup and cache-aware routing. Important to note: quantization reduces model memory footprint so effective KV cache size per GPU increases, which can improve performance if you get more cache hits. But also some quant formats increase KV cache CPU<->GPU copy overhead if the runtime handles decoder differently.
[03:28] Priya Nair: Can you elaborate on KV cache hit rate interactions?
[03:32] Maya Patel: Sure. If your inference pattern is many short context requests with overlapping prefixes, a larger KV cache per device (thanks to quant) means more entries can stay on-GPU, fewer remote fetches, lower latency. However if the runtime stores cache in FP16 on GPU but model weights are INT8, we need conversions in the attention path which can add overhead. Our runtime supports mixed paths but there are tradeoffs; we typically benchmark with simulated traffic.
[03:58] Jordan Lee: Quick interjection — we also have the Redwood Optimize suggestions that can auto-tune batching and cache parameters based on traces. We can run that against your trace if you share it.
[04:08] Alex Chen: We'll share a week's trace, but anonymized — should be fine.
[04:12] Maya Patel: Great. Moving on — tooling: GPTQ conversion is relatively stable; we have automated scripts that will do the per-channel rounding and compute bias corrections. AWQ conversions sometimes need layer-wise manual tuning and some layers you may want to leave in FP16 (e.g., final layernorm), especially if you see specific token-level regressions.
[04:34] Tom Ruiz: Are there specific patterns where AWQ fails?
[04:37] Maya Patel: On models with lots of narrow outlier weights or very sensitive embeddings, AWQ may require higher calibration samples; sometimes you see hallucination style regressions on rare tokens. That's why we do both intrinsic and task-level evals.
[04:54] Alex Chen: You mentioned hallucinations — in our system, false positives on command generation are critical. We can't accept even small increases.
[05:01] Maya Patel: Totally. For that class of safety-sensitive tasks we recommend a hybrid approach: quantize most layers but keep critical layers in FP16 or use a mixed-precision profile that our tooling can create. Also we can run targeted regression tests on the command set.
[05:18] Priya Nair: From infra side: if we go Private deployment on-prem, can Redwood still run the AWQ conversion inside our environment? We cannot allow artifacts out.
[05:27] Jordan Lee: Yes, we can ship a secure conversion container and our SEs can run it inside your VPC. We have an on-prem package for that exact use-case; we just need a little privileged access for the container to use the GPUs.
[05:39] Maya Patel: We'll need a calibration dataset for each quant method. For GPTQ usually 128-1k samples suffice depending on variance. For AWQ sometimes you need more. We'll propose a small sample and iterate.
[05:50] Alex Chen: If we run GPTQ and AWQ both, can we get per-prompt diff metrics?
[05:55] Maya Patel: Yes that's in the bench sheet — we provide diff columns: token-level divergence, perplexity delta, and task accuracy delta. We also produce a "regression hotspot" report which lists prompts where outputs diverge significantly.
[06:10] Tom Ruiz: What's typical magnitude of task accuracy delta? Is 1-2% common?
[06:14] Maya Patel: For many 13B variants, careful GPTQ can be <1% drop on task accuracy; AWQ can be similar or even better on some models. Worst case is several percent if you naively quantize everything. The goal is to find a minimal profile that meets your latency/cost targets with zero or near-zero task regressions.
[06:33] Jordan Lee: Also remember there are other knobs: intelligent batching, prefix caching, and routing to cheaper model variants under non-critical ops. For Peregrine, since commands are safety-sensitive, we can route those to a higher-precision model and non-critical logs to the quantized variant.
[06:47] Alex Chen: That routing idea is interesting — we currently don't have content-based routing. Is that supported?
[06:51] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood supports per-route model pinning, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback policies. You can classify requests at the edge and route accordingly.
[06:59] Priya Nair: On network latencies — if we keep inference on-prem, we avoid cloud egress. But what about rolling updates and audit logs?
[07:07] Jordan Lee: Private deployment includes an audit log collector that ships to your SIEM optionally, and rollouts can be controlled via canaries inside the VPC. We can also integrate with your KMS for key management.
[07:18] Alex Chen: Back to runtime specifics — you mentioned dequant overhead. Could that be mitigated by fused kernels?
[07:23] Maya Patel: Exactly. Our runtime has fused dequant + matmul kernels for certain arch/kernels. If your hardware supports the fused fp8 path (some newer GPUs do) the overhead is minimal. If not, you may pay extra cycles. We'll test on your exact hardware.
[07:37] Tom Ruiz: For our edge boxes, we have RTX 6000 Ada GPUs in the larger robots and older T4s in smaller ones. How much variance do you expect across those?
[07:45] Maya Patel: Quite a bit. Ada series with fp8 support will run FP8 faster; T4s are more limited so INT8 may be the better path there. Typically we recommend a heterogeneous strategy: use FP8/INT8 on Ada-class and INT8 on T4, with model variant pinning.
[08:00] Alex Chen: So we'd maintain multiple quantized artifacts per platform? That's extra ops overhead.
[08:06] Maya Patel: Yes, but Redwood Dedicated/Private handles artifact cataloging and model versioning so ops overhead is manageable. Also packing fewer variants is possible with mixed precision choices, but often the perf wins justify the slightly higher artifact count.
[08:20] Jordan Lee: Note: we can also generate a "downgrade" plan: if a quantized variant regresses in canary, automatic rollback to FP16 is supported.
[08:29] Priya Nair: Good. About canaries — do they support traffic mirroring so we can compare outputs live without user impact?
[08:35] Maya Patel: Yes, we support shadow mode and mirrored traffic so you can observe divergence without serving the quant output to the user. That's a recommended step for safety-sensitive models.
[08:46] Alex Chen: Let's talk about metrics — you said perplexity and token-level divergence. For commands we care about classification accuracy and false positive rate. Can Redwood run those task-level evals?
[08:55] Maya Patel: Absolutely. We'll run your command classification eval and return a ROC/PR curve and false positive delta. Our bench sheet will include both intrinsic and task-level metrics.
[09:05] Tom Ruiz: Any recommended baseline thresholds for rolling? Like don't push if FPR increases >0.5%?
[09:10] Maya Patel: It's customer dependent but for control commands we'd recommend near-zero tolerance; many customers set a very low threshold (<0.1%) and require human signoff. We'll codify thresholds in the runbook.
[09:21] Jordan Lee: Ok we should capture the immediate experiment — Plan A: run GPTQ with 512 calibration samples, keep output layers in FP16, measure task accuracy and p95; Plan B: run AWQ full conversion and compare. Maya will run a smoke test.
[09:35] Maya Patel: I'll add one more note — quantization can change logits subtly which may increase hallucination in generative tasks. For retrieval/classification tasks it's usually safer, but for generation you have to look carefully at token distribution.
[09:48] Alex Chen: Our command generator is constrained to a small vocab and beam width 1, so hopefully fewer issues.
[09:54] Priya Nair: For bench execution inside our VPC, what resources do you need?
[09:58] Maya Patel: Ideally a single Ada GPU for the full run and a T4 for the smaller variant, some container runtime and about 50GB disk for artifacts. We'll provide an image.
[10:09] Alex Chen: We can provision that.
[10:12] Maya Patel: Great. A few real-world notes from other customers: we saw a case where naive INT8 caused a 3% drop in named-entity extraction because the embedding layer sensitivity; solution was mixed-precision and re-embedding the top tokens. Another customer used AWQ and got equivalent task accuracy and 30% latency improvement on their fp8-capable hardware. So results vary.
[10:37] Tom Ruiz: That tracks. Anything else we'd do to reduce p95 jitter?
[10:42] Maya Patel: Tuned prewarm, small batch sizes, and always use prefix caching where possible. Also avoid large dynamic shape overhead; pad to reasonable limits. Redwood runtime has a latency-optimized profile we can enable for those routes.
[10:55] Alex Chen: On auditing — if we have an incident, do you provide logs that map request->model_version->quant_profile?
[11:01] Jordan Lee: Yes, audit logs include model artifact id, quant profile tag, and route/trace id. Those go to your SIEM if configured.
[11:08] Priya Nair: About license/compliance — AWQ/GPTQ conversions use some 3rd-party libs; any IP worries?
[11:13] Jordan Lee: We provide a legal summarization in the security pack. For on-prem conversions we can run open-source tools entirely inside your environment; we don't retain derived artifacts unless you ask. We'll include license notes.
[11:25] Maya Patel: Wrapping up technical recommendations: start with GPTQ on your Ada hardware with a hybrid keep-list for critical layers, run AWQ as a compare, measure task accuracy and FPR on the command dataset, and use shadow mode and slow canary before full rollout.
[11:42] Alex Chen: Sounds like a plan. Regarding timeline, we aim to have a bench run completed in the week after next.
[11:47] Jordan Lee: We'll send calendar invites; propose Jan 25th for the hands-on run.
[11:51] Maya Patel: I'll also share a sample bench config and the conversion container image.
[11:56] Tom Ruiz: Thanks — one last question: any guidance on cost delta? If we quantize, do you expect infra cost to drop 30-50%?
[12:02] Jordan Lee: Broadly yes; quantized artifacts reduce memory footprint and can increase GPU utilization. Customers report 20-50% TCO reduction depending on scale and hardware. We'll put expected ranges in the benchmark sheet tailored to your fleet.
[12:16] Alex Chen: Great.
[12:18] Jordan Lee: Ok let's do next steps and action items—Jordan will share bench sheet and deck by Jan 20, Maya will run smoke on the sample model, Alex will share prompts and traces, Priya will provide infra details.

[12:35] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. End of recording.
